notes.text: A kitchen so small you couldn't open the oven and the silverware drawer at the same time. That was the metaphor. It took them a while to see it. Once they did, they bought a château with a bread oven that predates the United States.
There's a historical record of a hidden underground tunnel running from their château to a neighboring town. They haven't found it yet. This is just a thing about their house.

"Rent before you buy" is the most underrated advice in travel writing. Two and a half years living on someone else's château grounds before committing to their own. That's not hesitation. That's how you avoid a very expensive mistake.

The French don't care if your five-year-old is reading yet. Formal reading doesn't start until six. By seven they're fluent anyway. Meanwhile American parents are panicking about kindergarten benchmarks. Maybe we're the ones doing it wrong.

They walked into their private forest one morning in April and found a carpet of bluebells — wall to wall, as far as you could see. Not in the listing. Not in the brochure. The realtor never mentioned it. They just stood there with their mouths open.
The fine print in France is written in invisible ink.
At what point does "this apartment is too small" become "we should probably move to France and buy a château"?

Things nobody tells you about château hunting:
— The price is never the whole price
— You will fall in love with forty of them before closing one deal
— A farmer's ancient land rights can transfer to his children indefinitely
— "Livable" means something very specific and you have to learn it the hard way
The life you dream about is sometimes the one you have to actually go build. Nobody is going to hand it to you pre-assembled with good lighting.

Kamille mentioned almost in passing that her neighbor's business card still had his ex-wife's name on it — just one thick line through it — and I knew that detail was going in the piece. Some people are a sentence.
